title: State rules under the Labour Codes: where the fine print lives
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Labour is a shared subject. Why State rules under the four Labour Codes decide thresholds, forms and procedures, where things stand, and how unions can take part.
body:
When people talk about the four Labour Codes, they usually talk about the headline changes: a floor wage, gratuity for fixed-term employees, social security for gig workers, a single registration. But a Code is only the skeleton of a law. The muscle and the nerves are in the **rules** made under it, and because labour is a shared subject in India's federal structure, a large share of those rules is made by State Governments, not by the Centre. For a worker or a union office-bearer in a State, the rules of that State are often the document that decides what actually happens at the factory gate.

## Why the States have a say

The Constitution's Seventh Schedule has three lists. Labour matters sit mainly in List III, the Concurrent List, where both Parliament and State legislatures can act. Entry 22 of that list covers trade unions and industrial and labour disputes. Entry 23 covers social security and social insurance, and employment and unemployment. Entry 24 covers the welfare of labour, including conditions of work and provident funds ([Constitution of India, Concurrent List](https://constitutionofindia.net/schedules/list-iii-concurrent-list/)).

Because of this, each Code uses the idea of an "appropriate Government". For some establishments, such as railways, mines, banking, insurance and central public sector undertakings, the appropriate Government is the Centre. For most other employers, including the vast majority of factories, shops, small units and contractors in a State, it is the State Government. A report on the Central rules makes this point directly: the Central rules apply where the Centre is the appropriate Government, and other employers must follow their State's rules ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)).

## What has happened so far

The four Codes (Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions) were brought into force by the Centre on 21 November 2025. According to the Government, they consolidate 29 earlier Central labour laws ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/labour-codes-labour-laws-ministry-of-labour-central-govt-125112100754_1.html)). The Labour Ministry's guidance explained that during the transition, existing rules continue to operate to the extent they are consistent with the Codes, until new rules are notified ([SCC Online report on the Ministry's FAQs](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)).

The Centre then pre-published draft rules on 31 December 2025. Stakeholders were given 30 days to comment on the Industrial Relations Code and 45 days on the other three Codes ([The Week, reporting PTI](https://www.theweek.in/wire-updates/business/2025/12/31/centre-pre-publishes-draft-rules-on-four-labour-codes-to-seek-stakeholders-feedback.html)). The final Central rules followed on 8 and 9 May 2026, together with Model Standing Orders ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)).

State rules are following at different speeds. A tracker published by a law firm in May 2026 showed a patchwork: a handful of States and Union Territories, among them Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar and Gujarat, were listed as having notified rules under all four Codes, while many others were still at the draft stage ([Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan tracker](https://employmentlaw.lkslaw.com/rules)). The tracker itself warns that readers should verify each State's status against the official gazette, and the same advice applies to anything you read here, since the position changes month by month.

For West Bengal, a Business Today report of 8 July 2026 said the State Government had begun discussing how to implement and notify the Codes and was expected to start drafting rules shortly. The same report noted that Karnataka and Maharashtra had notified some provisions even before the Centre did ([Business Today](https://www.businesstoday.in/latest/economy/story/west-bengal-government-set-to-implement-labour-codes-541845-2026-07-08)).

## What the rules actually decide

It helps to see how much is left to rules. The Central rules, for example, fix a good deal of practical detail:

- The format of the **appointment letter**, which must carry the establishment's labour identification number and the employee's Universal Account Number.
- Limits on **deductions** from wages: the Code caps total deductions at 50 per cent of wages, and the rules require the employer to give the employee seven days to explain before deducting for damage or loss.
- Rules on **overtime**, including a cap of 144 hours per quarter and payment at twice the normal rate.
- **Facilities**: canteens where 100 workers are employed, welfare officers at 250, ambulance rooms at 500, and crèche requirements in building work above 50 workers.
- The procedure for **recognising a negotiating union**, including a secret-ballot verification of membership, and the facilities, such as office space, that establishments with 300 or more workers must give.
- **Registration** through an online portal, with deemed registration after seven days.

These details come from reports on the Central rules ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers); [Mondaq, "Cracking the Code II"](https://www.mondaq.com/india/employee-rights-labour-relations/1807196/cracking-the-code-ii-the-new-central-labour-rules-at-a-glance)). They bind only the establishments for which the Centre is the appropriate Government. A State is free to prescribe its own thresholds, forms and time limits for everyone else, so a canteen threshold, a crèche requirement or the procedure for recognising a union can differ from one State to another. The reports also say that many States had published draft rules, which means the numbers above are a guide to what to look for, not a promise of what your State will adopt.

## Why it matters to workers and unions

A progressive Code can be thinned out by narrow rules, and a cautious Code can be strengthened by careful ones. Consider the plain-language questions a worker asks. Will I get a proper appointment letter? How long can my employer take to answer a complaint? Which office do I go to if my wages are delayed? Who verifies the membership of my union? Every one of these is answered, at least in part, in the rules.

There is also a very practical reason for unions to read State rules closely. An employer operating in two States may find that it must follow one set of thresholds in one State and another in the second. A union that works across States, or a federation, needs to know both. Differences are not wrong in themselves, since the Constitution allows States to respond to local conditions, but they should be known and, where they reduce a protection the Code intends, they should be raised.

## What BMS has said and done

BMS has welcomed the Codes while asking for changes in some provisions. In a statement of 31 January 2026 it described the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security as historic and revolutionary, while stating its concerns on provisions in the other two Codes ([BMS statement](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=9332)). In August 2025, its Central Executive had already asked the Government to roll out the Codes in phases with tripartite consultation ([BMS press release](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=8936)). At its All India Working Committee at Ranchi on 26 to 28 July 2026, BMS decided to formally submit suggestions and objections on the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code ([Organiser](https://organiser.org/2026/07/29/372464/bharat/jharkhand-bms-national-working-committee-meeting-concludes-calls-for-eps-pension-hike-amendments-to-labour-codes/)). That is where State-level work becomes important, because the objections must reach the people who actually draft the State rules.

## How to take part

1. **Find out the status.** Check your State labour department's website and gazette for draft or final rules under each of the four Codes.
2. **Compare.** Put the State draft next to the Central rules. Look for differences in thresholds, time limits, the form of documents and the authorities named.
3. **Write a short, specific objection or suggestion** within the date given in the draft notice. Name the rule, say what you want changed, and explain why in one or two sentences.
4. **Ask for a hearing.** Request your State's tripartite body, or the Labour Minister's office, to take up the points with unions and employers together.
5. **Keep proof of submission** and follow up. If the final rules ignore a point, you have a record to return to.

## What remains to be done

Many States have yet to complete their rules, and the first anniversary of the Codes is close. Until a State's rules are final, the transition provision means older rules continue where consistent, which can leave workers unsure which set applies. Units of BMS are well placed to help here. A karyakarta with legal training, or an advocate who works with the union, can read a draft in an evening and produce a useful note. That is the humble but decisive work that turns a law on paper into a right in practice.
